claim: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet learn powerful representations that support not only object recognition, but multiple other tasks like object detection, segmentation, and retrieval.
source: Computational work has shown that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet learn powerful representations that support not only object recognition, but multiple other tasks like object detection, segmentation, and retrieval (Liu et al., 2015; Golub et al., 2020; Babenko et al., 2014; Razavian et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Liu et al., 2015; Golub et al., 2020; Babenko et al., 2014; Razavian et al., 2014) that have demonstrated these capabilities.

claim: Several studies have claimed that CNNs can accurately predict scene stability.
source: Indeed, several studies have claimed that these networks can accurately predict scene stability (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016) that have made this claim.

claim: CNNs have so far been tested only within very narrow domains for stability prediction.
source: But CNNs have so far been tested only within very narrow domains (e.g., block towers with several cubes of different colors, in Figure 1A, left column) and it is not clear they would successfully predict future states of complex natural images (e.g., Figure 1A, middle two columns).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of prior work and is illustrated with reference to Figure 1A showing the difference between narrow domains (block towers) and complex natural images.

claim: A general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios may require a richer representation of the physical properties of the scene that support forward simulations like those in the physics engines of video games.
source: A general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios may instead require a richer representational of the physical properties of the scene that support forward simulations like those in the physics engines of video games (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017) that have proposed this hypothesis.

claim: Human observers can perceive stability extremely rapidly and preattentively.
source: On the one hand, human observers can perceive the stability extremely rapidly and preattentively (Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Yang and Wolfe, 2020), and these findings have been taken to argue for a simple feedforward rather than a simulation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Yang and Wolfe, 2020) that have demonstrated this capability.

claim: Human judgments of the stability of a tower of blocks are well modeled by approximate probabilistic simulation in game-style physics engines.
source: On the other hand, human judgments of the stability of a tower of blocks are well modeled by approximate probabilistic simulation in game-style physics engines (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017), which better fit the human pattern of errors than CNNs do (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017) that have demonstrated this modeling approach.

claim: Physics engine models better fit the human pattern of errors in stability judgments than CNNs do.
source: On the other hand, human judgments of the stability of a tower of blocks are well modeled by approximate probabilistic simulation in game-style physics engines (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017), which better fit the human pattern of errors than CNNs do (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study (Zhang et al., 2016) that compared these models.

claim: Humans can easily judge the physical stability of a wide variety of novel real-world images.
source: Perhaps most importantly, humans can easily judge the physical stability of a wide variety of novel real-world images, which is likely to require a more abstract and generalizable representation of physical properties of the scene.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about human capabilities and is used to motivate the study.

claim: The ventral visual pathway has long been implicated in visual object recognition.
source: However, in frontoparietal regions previously implicated in intuitive physical reasoning we find both scenario-invariant representations of physical stability, and higher univariate responses to unstable than stable scenes. These results demonstrate abstract representations of physical stability in the dorsal but not ventral pathway, consistent with the hypothesis that the computations underlying stability entail not just pattern classification but forward physical simulation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the ventral visual pathway's role in object recognition.

claim: Frontoparietal regions have been previously implicated in intuitive physical reasoning.
source: However, in frontoparietal regions previously implicated in intuitive physical reasoning we find both scenario-invariant representations of physical stability, and higher univariate responses to unstable than stable scenes.
evidence: The claim is based on prior research that has implicated these regions in physical reasoning, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: Within each scenario (Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People), a linear SVM classifier trained on ResNet-50 features showed above chance classification accuracy for distinguishing stable from unstable images.
source: These analyses replicated previous results by showing above chance classification accuracy within the Block Towers scenario and further found higher classification performance within our two new natural image sets (60.1%, 75%, and 71.4% for Block Towers, Physical-Objects, and Physical-People scenarios, respectively; diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p < 0.05 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing classification accuracies and statistical significance, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Classification accuracy for stability did not generalize across scenarios when training and testing on different scenarios.
source: However, this performance did not generalize across scenarios: accuracy was near chance for all cross-validation tests in which the SVM classifier was trained on one scenario and tested on a different scenario (i.e., off-diagonal cells in Figure 1B, p > 0.15 for a bootstrap test with n = 10,000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing near-chance accuracies for cross-scenario tests, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Visual features from feedforward deep CNNs do not carry abstract and generalizable information about physical stability.
source: Thus, visual features from this feedforward deep CNN do not carry abstract and generalizable information about physical stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing lack of cross-scenario generalization.

claim: The fact that CNN features can distinguish stability within a scenario but not across scenarios suggests that the discriminative features might be related to incidental properties indicative of stability only within a particular scenario.
source: The fact that these CNN features can distinguish stability within a scenario but not across scenarios suggests that the discriminative features underlying this discrimination might be related to incidental properties that are indicative of stability only within a particular scenario (e.g., the displacement of each block from the centroid of the block below).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results about what the CNN features might be capturing.

claim: All participants had significant voxels within both VTC and physics parcels.
source: All participants had significant voxels within both VTC and physics parcels (number of voxels per participant, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM] =350.5 ± 68.7 for VTC ROIs and mean ± SEM =311.3 ± 69.8 for physics ROIs).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on the number of voxels identified in each participant.

claim: In VTC, within condition pattern correlations were significantly higher than between condition pattern correlations for both Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios.
source: For VTC, we found that the within condition pattern correlations were significantly higher than the between condition pattern correlations for both Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios (see Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating the presence of information about stability for each scenario type.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing pattern correlation differences, as shown in Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In VTC, pattern information did not distinguish perilous from nonperilous situations in the Animals-People scenarios.
source: However, pattern information did not distinguish perilous (or 'unstable') from nonperilous ('stable') situations in the Animals-People scenarios (see Figure 3 for stats).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of significant differences, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: In VTC, there was a significant interaction between scenario type and within versus between correlations.
source: Further, this difference in stability information across scenario types was itself significant, as revealed by a significant interaction between-scenario type and within versus between correlations in an analysis of variance (ANOVA) (F1,12 = 72.2, p = 0.000002).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the experimental data.

claim: The Physics Network showed significantly higher correlations within than between stability for both the Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not the Animals-People scenarios.
source: The Physics Network showed the same pattern of results (Figures 2B and 3), with significantly higher correlations within than between stability for both the Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not the Animals-People scenarios, and a significant ANOVA interaction between-scenario type and within versus between correlations (F1,12 = 22.9, p = 0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing pattern correlation differences, as shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: Both VTC and the Physics Network contain information about physical (but not animate) stability when analyzed within scenarios.
source: Thus, both VTC and the Physics Network contain information about physical (but not animate) stability when analyzed within scenarios.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential responses to physical versus animate scenarios.

claim: In the Physics Network, within condition pattern correlations are significantly higher than between condition pattern correlations only across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, but not across Physical and Animate scenarios.
source: Indeed, we found that in the Physics Network (and not in VTC – see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), the within condition pattern correlations are significantly higher than between condition pattern correlations only across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, but not across Physical and Animate scenarios (Figures 2D and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing cross-scenario pattern correlation differences, as shown in Figures 2D and 3.

claim: There was a significant interaction between fROI (physics vs. VTC) and between-scenario stability information, indicating stronger generalization across scenarios in the Physics Network compared to the VTC fROI.
source: Further, we found a significant interaction between fROI (physics vs. VTC) and between-scenario stability information (within vs. between correlations), indicating stronger generalization across scenarios in the Physics Network compared to the VTC fROI (F1,12 = 6.29, p = 0.027).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing the two brain regions.

claim: The Physics Network holds information about physical stability that generalizes from scenarios with only inanimate objects to scenarios in which people are in physically unstable situations, but not to scenarios in which people are in peril from animals.
source: Thus, the Physics Network (and not VTC) holds information about physical stability that generalizes from scenarios with only inanimate objects to scenarios in which people are in physically unstable situations, but not to scenarios in which people are in peril from animals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective generalization across physical but not animate scenarios.

claim: None of the eye movement quantities showed a significant difference between stable and unstable conditions in any of the scenarios except for saccade amplitude in the 'Physical-People' scenario.
source: None of these quantities showed a significant difference between stable and unstable conditions in any of the scenarios except for saccade amplitude in the 'Physical-People' scenario (p = 0.028, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of eye movement data collected during the experiment.

claim: There was no significant interaction of stability with scenario type for any of the eye movement quantities.
source: However, we found no significant interaction of stability with scenario type for any of the eye movement quantities using separate ANOVAs (p > 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of eye movement data.

claim: The observed differences in brain activations for the stimulus conditions are unlikely to be explained by differences in retinal input patterns due to eye movements.
source: Thus, the observed differences in brain activations for our stimulus conditions are unlikely to be explained by differences in retinal input patterns due to eye movements.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the eye movement analysis showing no systematic differences.

claim: Subjective ratings of 'interestingness' revealed significantly higher ratings for unstable over stable conditions in all three scenarios.
source: Second, analysis of subjective ratings by a separate set of subjects (see Methods) of 'interestingness' of our stimuli (which we used as a proxy for how attention-grabbing the stimuli were) revealed significantly higher ratings for unstable over stable conditions in all three scenarios (p < 0.001 for a paired t-test on average ratings across subjects; Supplementary file 1, last column).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from a separate rating experiment.

claim: There was no interaction between stability and scenario type in the interestingness ratings.
source: However, we found no interaction between stability and scenario type in the ANOVA (p = 0.23), implying that the difference in ratings between stability conditions did not vary between physical and animate scenarios.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the rating data.

claim: The distinctive and generalizable representation of physical stability found in the Physics Network are unlikely to be due to differential eye movements, attention, or difficulty confounds.
source: Thus, the distinctive and generalizable representation of physical stability we found in the Physics Network are unlikely to be due to differential eye movements, attention, or difficulty confounds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control analyses showing no systematic confounds.

claim: An ANOVA analyzing the generalization of stability information did not find a significant interaction of stability information with either hemisphere or lobe.
source: An ANOVA analyzing the generalization of stability information (between vs. within condition pattern correlations across Physical-Objects and Physical-People; F1,12 = 6.11, p = 0.03 for the main effect) did not find a significant interaction of stability information with either hemisphere (left vs. right; F1,12 = 2.75, p = 0.12) or lobe (parietal vs. frontal; F1,12 = 0.24, p = 0.63; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of subregions within the Physics Network.

claim: The stability information was stronger in the parietal compared with frontal lobe.
source: However, the stability information was stronger in the parietal compared with frontal lobe (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of subregions showing differential effects.

claim: In both V1 and LOC, significant decoding of stability was found only in Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios.
source: In both regions, we found significant decoding of stability only in Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-decoding of stability across physical scenarios (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing pattern analysis results in V1 and LOC, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The interaction of cross-decoding effect with fROI was significant in separate ANOVAs contrasting the Physics Network with V1 and LOC.
source: In addition, the interaction of this cross-decoding effect with fROI was significant in separate ANOVAs contrasting the Physics Network with V1 (F1,12 = 6.31, p = 0.027) and LOC (F1,12 = 5.63, p = 0.035).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing different brain regions.

claim: A generalizable representation of physical stability is apparently a distinctive property of the Physics Network in the parietal and frontal lobes and is not a widespread property of visual cortex.
source: Thus, a generalizable representation of physical stability is apparently a distinctive property of the Physics Network in the parietal and frontal lobes and is not a widespread property of visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective effects in the Physics Network compared to visual regions.

claim: The physically unstable condition showed a significantly greater response compared to the physically stable condition in both 'Physical-Objects' and 'Physical-People' scenarios in the Physics Network.
source: As predicted, the physically unstable condition showed a significantly greater response compared to the physically stable condition in both 'Physical-Objects' (p = 0.02 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects) and 'Physical-People' scenarios (p = 0.04 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects; Figures 4 and 5, left column), but not the 'Animals-People' scenario (p = 0.66 for a paired t-test on average response across subjects; Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing univariate response differences, as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: There was a significant interaction between stability and lobe but not hemisphere for the 'Physical-Objects' scenarios in the Physics Network.
source: We found a significant interaction between stability (unstable vs. stable) and lobe (F1,12 = 8.28, p = 0.014) but not hemisphere (F1,12 = 3.04, p = 0.11) for the 'Physical-Objects' scenarios, and the same pattern for the 'Physical-People' scenario (stability × lobe: F1,12 = 8.53, p = 0.013; stability × hemisphere: F1,12 = 0.34, p = 0.57).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of subregions within the Physics Network.

claim: The interaction effect between stability and lobe was largely driven by the univariate difference in the parietal but not frontal lobe.
source: Post hoc analysis revealed that this interaction effect was largely driven by the univariate difference in the parietal but not frontal lobe (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by post hoc analysis of the ANOVA results.

claim: VTC and other visual regions (V1 and LOC) did not show higher responses for unstable than stable conditions.
source: According to our hypothesis, it is the automatic simulation occurring in the Physics Network that leads to the higher response for unstable than stable conditions. As such we predicted that we would not see this same effect in VTC and other visual regions (V1 and LOC) that are not engaged in physical simulation. Indeed, as shown in Figure 5, we did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of univariate differences in visual regions, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. visual fROI) for the 'Physical-Objects' and 'Physical-People' scenarios.
source: Furthermore, we found a significant interaction of stability with region (physics fROI vs. visual fROI) for the 'Physical-Objects' (F1,12 = 13.04, p = 0.0035 for V1; F1,12 = 8.27, p = 0.014 for VTC) and the 'Physical-People' scenarios (F1,12 = 11.14, p = 0.0059 for V1; F1,12 = 7.83, p = 0.016 for LOC).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) comparing physics and visual regions.

claim: Physically unstable scenes evoke stronger responses than stable scenes in the frontoparietal Physics Network, but not elsewhere, consistent with the hypothesis that these regions are engaged in running forward simulations of what will happen next.
source: Thus, physically unstable scenes evoke stronger responses than stable scenes in the frontoparietal Physics Network, but not elsewhere, consistent with the hypothesis that these regions are engaged in running forward simulations of what will happen next.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective univariate effects in the Physics Network.

claim: Visual motion area MT showed significantly higher responses for unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes for all three types of scenarios.
source: As shown in Figures 3 and 5 (last column), we found significantly higher responses in MT for unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes for all three types of scenarios without any significant stability information in the pattern activations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing univariate response differences in MT, as shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The increased response to conditions with predicted motion in MT is reminiscent of previous reports showing greater response in MT for static images with implied motion.
source: This increased response to conditions with predicted motion is reminiscent of previous reports showing greater response in MT for static images with implied motion (Kourtzi and Kanwisher, 2000).
evidence: The claim draws a comparison to prior research (Kourtzi and Kanwisher, 2000) on MT responses to implied motion.

claim: The current study shows activation of MT for motion that is only predicted (in the Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios), whereas the earlier study reported higher responses in MT for static images depicting motion events happening at the moment the photograph was taken.
source: The critical difference, however, is that whereas the earlier study reported higher responses in MT for static images depicting motion events happening at the moment the photograph was taken (implied motion) the current study shows activation of MT for motion that is only predicted (in the Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios).
evidence: The claim contrasts the current findings with prior research to highlight a novel aspect of the results.

claim: The lack of univariate difference for the Animals-People scenario in the Physics ROI suggests that the Physics Network is not merely responding to general 'likeliness to change' or predicted motion.
source: Most importantly, the lack of this univariate difference for the Animals-People scenario in the Physics ROI suggests that the Physics Network is not merely responding to general 'likeliness to change' or predicted motion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective responses to physical but not animate scenarios.

claim: Frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference contain abstract information about physical stability.
source: Here, we report that frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference contain abstract information about physical stability, but representations in the ventral visual object recognition pathway, and those in feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition, do not.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Representations in the ventral visual object recognition pathway do not contain abstract information about physical stability.
source: Here, we report that frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference contain abstract information about physical stability, but representations in the ventral visual object recognition pathway, and those in feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition, do not.
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Representations in feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition do not contain abstract information about physical stability.
source: Here, we report that frontoparietal cortical regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference contain abstract information about physical stability, but representations in the ventral visual object recognition pathway, and those in feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition, do not.
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Representations in systems that are highly effective at invariant object recognition do not automatically support the general ability to distinguish physically stable from unstable scenes.
source: Our results indicate that representations in systems that are highly effective at invariant object recognition do not automatically support the general ability to distinguish physically stable from unstable scenes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing lack of generalization in CNNs and ventral pathway.

claim: The ability to distinguish physically stable from unstable scenes in humans is supported by a different system in the dorsal visual pathway that has been previously implicated in intuitive physical inference.
source: Instead, this ability in humans is supported by a different system in the dorsal visual pathway that has been previously implicated in intuitive physical inference.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective effects in the Physics Network.

claim: The Physics Network shows a higher univariate response to unstable than stable scenes, as predicted if it performs forward simulations of what will happen next.
source: This Physics Network (but not the ventral pathway) further shows a higher univariate response to unstable than stable scenes, as predicted if it performs forward simulations of what will happen next.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and interpreted in light of the simulation hypothesis.

claim: Neither pattern nor univariate information about physical stability in the Physics Network can be straightforwardly accounted for by low-level visual features, differential eye movements or attention.
source: Control analyses confirmed that neither pattern nor univariate information about physical stability in the Physics Network can be straightforwardly accounted for by low-level visual features, differential eye movements or attention.
evidence: The claim is based on control analyses showing no systematic confounds.

claim: The human brain represents the physical world not via simple pattern classification but instead by building a model of the physical world that supports prediction via forward simulation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the human brain represents the physical world not via simple pattern classification but instead by building a model of the physical world that supports prediction via forward simulation.
evidence: The claim is a broad interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks.
source: Across multiple studies, similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to (1) respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks (Fischer et al., 2016), (2) represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli (Mason and Just, 2016), and (3) contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Fischer et al., 2016; Mason and Just, 2016; Schwettmann et al., 2019).

claim: Similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli.
source: Across multiple studies, similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to (1) respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks (Fischer et al., 2016), (2) represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli (Mason and Just, 2016), and (3) contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study (Mason and Just, 2016).

claim: Similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass.
source: Across multiple studies, similar frontoparietal regions have been shown to (1) respond more during physics-based tasks compared to color-based or social prediction tasks (Fischer et al., 2016), (2) represent physical concepts in verbal stimuli (Mason and Just, 2016), and (3) contain scenario-invariant representations of object mass (Schwettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study (Schwettmann et al., 2019).

claim: The regions activated during physical inference overlap with regions shown previously to be engaged during visually guided action and tool use.
source: Intriguingly, the regions activated during physical inference overlap with regions shown previously to be engaged during visually guided action (Goodale and Westwood, 2004) and tool use (Gallivan et al., 2013; Valyear et al., 2007; Mruczek et al., 2013), perhaps because these tasks also require a representation of the physical world.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Goodale and Westwood, 2004; Gallivan et al., 2013; Valyear et al., 2007; Mruczek et al., 2013).

claim: Physical simulation has been proposed as a crucial component in models for human-like robotic action planning and flexible tool use.
source: Indeed physical simulation has been proposed as a crucial component in models for human-like robotic action planning (Toussaint et al., 2018; Toussaint et al., 2020; Mordatch et al., 2012) and flexible tool use (Allen et al., 2020; Osiurak and Badets, 2016; Osiurak et al., 2020); plausibly the same brain mechanisms could have arisen or adapted to support all of these computations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Toussaint et al., 2018; Toussaint et al., 2020; Mordatch et al., 2012; Allen et al., 2020; Osiurak and Badets, 2016; Osiurak et al., 2020).

claim: The same brain mechanisms could have arisen or adapted to support physical simulation, action planning, and tool use.
source: Indeed physical simulation has been proposed as a crucial component in models for human-like robotic action planning (Toussaint et al., 2018; Toussaint et al., 2020; Mordatch et al., 2012) and flexible tool use (Allen et al., 2020; Osiurak and Badets, 2016; Osiurak et al., 2020); plausibly the same brain mechanisms could have arisen or adapted to support all of these computations.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the evolutionary or developmental origins of these brain mechanisms.

claim: The frontoparietal regions implicated in physical inference also overlap with the 'multiple demand' system and are unlikely to be selectively engaged in only physical inference.
source: Note however that these same regions also overlap with the 'multiple demand' system (Fischer et al., 2016), and are unlikely to be selectively engaged in only physical inference.
evidence: The claim is based on prior research (Fischer et al., 2016) showing overlap with the multiple demand system.

claim: The present study strengthens evidence that frontoparietal regions are engaged in intuitive physical inference by showing that they carry a new kind of physical information: the dynamic physical stability of objects and people in a scene.
source: In the present study, we strengthen evidence that these regions are engaged in intuitive physical inference by showing that they carry a new kind of physical information: the dynamic physical stability of objects and people in a scene.
evidence: The claim summarizes the contribution of the current study to the literature.

claim: Information about physical stability is present in the Physics Network when participants simply view images of physical scenes, even though they are not asked to judge stability.
source: Interestingly, this information is present when participants simply view images of physical scenes, even though they are not asked to judge stability.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design where participants performed a 1-back task rather than judging stability.

claim: It is a matter of active current debate in AI whether features extracted by feedforward computations in networks trained on visual object classification will suffice for physical inference, or whether richer internal models that support forward simulation are required.
source: More importantly, our work speaks not only to which brain regions are implicated in intuitive physical inference, but what kinds of computations these inferences entail in both minds and machines. In particular, it is a matter of active current debate in AI whether features extracted by feedforward computations in networks trained on visual object classification will suffice for physical inference, or whether richer internal models that support forward simulation are required.
evidence: The claim describes an ongoing debate in the AI literature.

claim: Some work has shown that CNNs can learn from extensive labeled datasets to infer the stability of block towers and predict future outcomes.
source: Some work has shown that CNNs can learn from extensive labeled datasets to infer the stability of block towers (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019) and predict future outcomes (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).

claim: CNNs tested on specific tasks and stimuli do not generalize across scenarios for the task of determining physical stability.
source: But these CNNs have so far been tested only on specific tasks and stimuli, and we show here that they do not generalize across scenarios for the task of determining physical stability.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the CNN analysis in the current study.

claim: It has been proposed that a general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios will require a more structured representation of the physical world that will support forward simulation.
source: Instead, it has been proposed that a general ability to predict what will happen next in physical scenarios will require a more structured representation of the physical world that will support forward simulation (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017).

claim: A parallel debate is occurring in cognitive science between those who argue that human physical inferences are computed by pattern recognition versus those who argue they are best accounted for by mental simulation.
source: A parallel debate is raging in cognitive science (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Battaglia et al., 2013; Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Firestone and Scholl, 2016; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2019; Davis and Marcus, 2015; Chater and Oaksford, 2017; Davis et al., 2017; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2020), between those who argue that because human physical inferences occur rapidly (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) and preattentively (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) they are computed by something like a pattern recognition process, versus those who argue that human and primate physical inference behavior is best accounted for by mental simulation (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017; Rajalingham et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim describes an ongoing debate in cognitive science and is supported by citations to multiple studies on both sides.

claim: Three lines of evidence from the present study indicate that pattern recognition alone is unlikely to explain physical inference in humans for the case of physical stability.
source: Three lines of evidence from the present study indicate that pattern recognition alone – as instantiated in feedforward CNNs and the ventral visual pathway – is unlikely to explain physical inference in humans, at least for the case of physical stability.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusions drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The present study finds generalizable representations of physical stability in the brain that are not found in CNNs.
source: First, we find generalizable representations of physical stability in the brain that we do not find in CNNs.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the experimental results.

claim: Abstract representations of stability are not found in the ventral visual pathway but rather in the dorsal pathway, previously implicated in intuitive physical inference.
source: Second, these abstract representations of stability are not found in the ventral visual pathway, which is thought to conduct pattern classification and is well modeled by CNNs, but rather in the dorsal pathway, previously implicated in intuitive physical inference.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the experimental results.

claim: The present study finds a higher univariate response in the Physics Network for unstable scenes, where there is more to simulate, than stable scenes, where nothing is predicted to happen next.
source: Third, we find a higher univariate response in this Physics Network for unstable scenes, where there is more to simulate, than the stable scenes, where nothing is predicted to happen next.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the experimental results.

claim: The hypothesis pertains only to feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition (on ImageNet dataset).
source: However, note that our hypothesis pertains only to feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition (on ImageNet dataset); It remains an open question whether a feedforward CNN extensively trained on naturalistic images of stability may learn generalizable representations of physical stability.
evidence: The claim clarifies the scope of the conclusions and acknowledges limitations.

claim: It remains an open question whether a feedforward CNN extensively trained on naturalistic images of stability may learn generalizable representations of physical stability.
source: However, note that our hypothesis pertains only to feedforward CNNs trained on object recognition (on ImageNet dataset); It remains an open question whether a feedforward CNN extensively trained on naturalistic images of stability may learn generalizable representations of physical stability.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation and suggests a direction for future research.

claim: Visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties.
source: We therefore hypothesize that visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties (see Almeida et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2011 for the cases of tool processing and visuospatial reasoning), and this representation is in turn used for forward simulation of what will happen next.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the relationship between ventral and dorsal pathways, supported by citations to related work (Almeida et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2011).

claim: An integrated computational model has been recently proposed that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model of object dynamics.
source: This idea has been recently proposed as an integrated computational model that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model of object dynamics, which then can be used to perceive, predict, reason about, and plan with physical objects (Yildirim et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work (Yildirim et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).

claim: Models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs should be able to make predictions of physical stability on realistic stimuli and form the basis for neurally mappable encoding models.
source: This class of models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs (Bear, 2020; Mrowca, 2018) should be able to make predictions of physical stability on the realistic stimuli used in our experiment and also form the basis for neurally mappable encoding models of the candidate physics regions.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential of certain computational models, supported by citations (Bear, 2020; Mrowca, 2018).

claim: The question of how such a model is instantiated in the brain remains unanswered and provides a fertile avenue for future exploration.
source: The question of how such a model is instantiated, if at all, in the brain remains unanswered and provides a fertile avenue for future exploration.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation and suggests a direction for future research.

source: We then tested each classifier on the remaining two scenarios to quantify cross-decoding of stability across scenarios. Here also, we found close to chance (=50%) cross-decoding performance (average % accuracy = 51.8% for Physical-Objects vs. Physical-People, 44.6% for Physical-Objects vs. Animals-People, and 41.1% for Physical-People vs. Animals-People).

source: To validate this measure, we also included high and low arousal images (n = 14 each) from IAPS (Lang et al., 1997) and obtained higher interestingness ratings for high arousal images compared to low arousal IAPS images (avg interestingness rating: high arousal images = 3.5 and low arousal images = 1.5; p < 0.000005).

source: This overlap map was spatially smoothed with a Gaussian filter (FWHM = 8 mm) and then thresholded so that the map contained only those voxels with at least 10% overlap across subjects.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the parcel definition procedure.

source: Then, the overlap map was divided into group-level parcels using a water-shed image segmentation algorithm (watershed function in MATLAB).

source: Finally, we selected a subset of parcels in which at least 16 out of the 27 (~60%) subjects show some activated voxels. This resulted in seven group-level parcels spanning frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes.

source: We defined fROI in each individual subject as the intersection of subject-specific localizer contrast map and group-level (or anatomical) parcels.

source: Specifically, we used the physics localizer to identify brain regions in each individual subject that responded more to the physics task compared to the color task (uncorrected p value <0.001 for the physics > color contrast).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the fROI definition procedure.

claim: The individual subject fROI contained only those voxels that showed significantly stronger activations for the physics task compared to the color task and fell within the group-level physics parcel.

evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the fROI definition procedure.

claim: This fROI definition procedure allowed the fROI locations and sizes to vary across subjects but restricted them to a common general region across subjects.
source: This allowed the fROI locations and sizes to vary across subjects but restricted them to a common general region across subjects.
evidence: The claim describes the rationale for the fROI definition procedure.

claim: fROIs for V1, LOC, and VTC were defined in each subject using a physics + color > fixation contrast intersected with anatomical masks.
source: In addition to the physics fROI, we also defined fROIs for the primary visual cortex (V1), LOC, and VTC in each subject. As before, we used data from the physics localizer to identify brain regions that responded to visual stimuli compared to fixation (uncorrected p value <0.001 for physics + color > fixation contrast). We then intersected this contrast map with masks derived from anatomical parcellation and considered only those significant voxels from the contrast map lying within the anatomical mask for further analyses.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the fROI definition procedure for visual regions.

claim: Area MT was localized using a standard localizer (coherent vs. random dot motion contrast) and included significant voxels within an anatomically defined mask.

claim: Within condition pattern correlations were computed as correlation between voxel activation patterns for even and odd runs, computed separately for unstable and stable conditions within a scenario.
source: In an fROI, we computed within condition pattern correlations (correlation between voxel activation patterns for even and odd runs, computed separately for unstable and stable conditions within a scenario) and between conditions pattern correlations (correlation between voxel activation patterns for even runs of unstable condition and odd runs of stable condition within a scenario, and vice versa).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the pattern correlation analysis procedure.

claim: Between condition pattern correlations were computed as correlation between voxel activation patterns for even runs of unstable condition and odd runs of stable condition within a scenario, and vice versa.
source: In an fROI, we computed within condition pattern correlations (correlation between voxel activation patterns for even and odd runs, computed separately for unstable and stable conditions within a scenario) and between conditions pattern correlations (correlation between voxel activation patterns for even runs of unstable condition and odd runs of stable condition within a scenario, and vice versa).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the pattern correlation analysis procedure.

claim: Within and between condition pattern correlations were computed for each scenario in each hemisphere in each subject and compared using statistical tests after Fisher transformation.
source: We computed the within and between condition pattern correlations for each scenario in each hemisphere in each subject and compared the magnitudes of correlations using appropriate statistical tests after transforming the correlations using Fisher transform (atanh function in MATLAB).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the pattern correlation analysis and statistical testing procedure.

claim: A significantly higher within condition pattern correlation compared to between condition pattern correlation indicates that unstable and stable conditions evoke distinctive voxel activation patterns in a given fROI.
source: A significantly higher within condition pattern correlation compared to between condition pattern correlation indicates that unstable and stable conditions evoke distinctive voxel activation patterns in a given fROI.

claim: By always comparing data across even and odd runs, the analysis avoids obscuring pattern information from temporal pattern drifts.
source: Note that by always comparing data across even and odd runs we avoid obscuring pattern information from temporal pattern drifts (Alink et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim describes the rationale for the analysis procedure, with citation to prior work.

claim: To explore the generalizability of neural representation of physical stability, multivoxel pattern correlations were computed across scenarios.
source: To explore the generalizability of neural representation of physical stability in a given fROI, we computed multivoxel pattern correlations computed across scenarios.

source: Specifically, in a given fROI, we extracted activation patterns for unstable and stable conditions from the two scenarios under consideration (say, 'Physical-Objects' and 'Physical-People' scenarios). We then computed pattern correlations between unstable (or stable) conditions across scenarios (within condition), and pattern correlations between unstable and stable conditions across scenarios (between condition).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the cross-scenario pattern correlation analysis procedure.

claim: Four pairwise pattern correlations were computed for each pair of categories within a given fROI in each hemisphere of each individual subject and transformed using Fisher transformation.
source: In this way, we computed the four pairwise pattern correlations for each pair of categories within a given fROI in each hemisphere of each individual subject and transformed them using Fisher transformation.

source: We compared the magnitudes of within and between condition correlations for each pair of categories across subjects using a paired t-test.
